job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: Political parties are organized groups that aim to win power to implement policies, but they are distinct from the government itself. While a party forms the government after winning an election, the government consists of the administrative machinery that runs the country, which remains even when parties change. To be recognized as a state party, a group must secure at least six percent of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a state and win at least two seats. Simply winning a few seats is insufficient for this official status. Regarding party systems, no single system is inherently superior; a multi-party system offers more choices but can lead to political instability, whereas a two-party system provides stability but limits voter options. Finally, internal democracy is a major concern in modern democracies. When leadership positions are passed down within a single family rather than through open elections, it creates dynastic succession. This practice is a significant challenge even in democratic nations, as it prevents new, talented members from rising to leadership roles, regardless of the country's overall democratic structure.

items.evidence: While a party forms the government after winning an election, the government consists of the administrative machinery that runs the country, which remains even when parties change.
items.q: Party A loses an election and Party B wins. What happens to the country's administrative machinery?
options: It keeps running the country under Party B
It ends, as Party A was the government
It is fully replaced by Party B's members
It stops until the next election is held
items.explain: The government's administrative machinery runs the country and remains even when the ruling party changes.

wrong.why: thinks the party and the government are the same
thinks the winning party's members become the whole machinery
thinks the machinery depends on a party being in power

items.evidence: To be recognized as a state party, a group must secure at least six percent of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a state and win at least two seats.
items.q: Which party meets the conditions to be recognised as a state party?
options: Party P: 7% of assembly votes, three seats
Party Q: 3% of assembly votes, five seats
Party R: 9% of assembly votes, one seat
Party S: 8% of city election votes, four seats
items.explain: A state party needs at least 6% of state assembly votes and at least two seats.

wrong.why: thinks winning a few seats is enough
thinks enough votes alone gives the status
thinks 6% of votes in any election counts

items.evidence: Regarding party systems, no single system is inherently superior; a multi-party system offers more choices but can lead to political instability, whereas a two-party system provides stability but limits voter options.
items.q: A country changes from a two-party to a multi-party system. What is likely to change?
options: Voters get more choices but less stability
Voters get more choices and more stability
Voters get fewer choices but more stability
Voters get the same choices but more stability
items.explain: A multi-party system offers more choices but can cause instability; no system is simply better.

wrong.why: thinks a multi-party system is better in every way
swaps the effects of the two systems
thinks the number of parties does not change voter options

items.evidence: This practice is a significant challenge even in democratic nations, as it prevents new, talented members from rising to leadership roles, regardless of the country's overall democratic structure.
items.q: In a democracy, a party's top post keeps passing from parent to child. What effect does this have?
options: It stops talented newcomers from becoming leaders
It causes no harm in a democratic country
It is fine, as voters still choose leaders
It gives the party more choices of leaders
items.explain: Dynastic succession is a challenge even in democracies because it keeps new, talented members from leading.

wrong.why: thinks dynasty is only a problem in monarchies
thinks elections make internal democracy unnecessary
reverses the effect stated in the passage
